                                        PROJECT NO. 58000


 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                           §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

 IN THE ERCOT REGION                            §



ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE’S COMMENTS AND PROPOSED REDLINES
          IN RESPONSE TO PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF
        AMENDMENTS TO §§ 25.192 AND 25.193 AND NEW § 25.252

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Rowan Digital Infrastructure (Rowan) files these comments and proposed redlines in

response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas’ (Commission) Proposal for Publication of

amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §§ 25.192 and 25.193 and new § 25.252

(PFP), and respectfully shows as follows:

                                  I.        INTRODUCTION

       Rowan develops large-scale digital infrastructure in the Electric Reliability Council of

Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) region and appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Commission’s

proposal to implement Section 6 of Senate Bill 6 (SB 6) by adopting new rules for transmission

cost recovery. Rowan’s portfolio includes major hyperscale data center campus projects under

construction in Temple and Medina County, Texas. Rowan’s portfolio in Temple includes six data

centers with a total minimum investment of $4.2 billion. Rowan’s minimum investment in Medina

County is $900 million and is expected to reach into the billions as the project progresses. Rowan

supports the Commission’s objective of assigning transmission costs in a manner that reflects cost

causation and urges the Commission to implement that objective consistent with the Legislature’s

direction in SB 6 that large load interconnection standards be designed to support business



                                                2
 development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and

maintaining system reliability.1 Rowan is a signatory of the White House Ratepayer Protection

Pledge2 and affirms its commitment to responsible data center development that supports grid

reliability and protects electricity ratepayers by ensuring new large load customers pay for all new

power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to serve data centers.

          As the Commission contemplates revisions to the PFP, Rowan asks the Commission to

consider that PURA requires rates to be sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each

customer class, and prohibits rates that are unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or

discriminatory.3 Rowan submits these comments because certain aspects of the PFP would not be

cost-based and would create a pancaking of charges and interconnection fees on large load

customers when read together with the requirements in Project No. 58481, Rulemaking to

Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards under PURA § 37.0561, and proposed 16 TAC

§ 25.194 (the “Large Load Interconnection Rule”).4 Read together, proposed §§ 25.192(b)(13),

25.192(e)(6), and 25.252(c)(2) would also operate to directly assign system upgrade costs to large

loads, which Rowan respectfully submits would have serious negative consequences for the

economic development in the state. Rowan fully supports safeguards to ensure that all ratepayers

pay for electric costs proportional to their demand.                      However, because the Large Load

Interconnection Rule would already require large loads to pay contributions in aid of construction

(CIAC) for their direct interconnection costs and to post financial security to cover system

2
    https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.
3
   PURA § 36.003(b). See also 16 TAC § 25.192(a) (“Each transmission service provider (TSP) shall file a tariff for

4
    See Project No. 58481, Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC § 25.194 (Mar. 12, 2026).

 upgrades, and because this PFP contemplates a minimum billing demand charge, a change of that

magnitude in the allocation of system upgrade costs is not necessary to protect other customer

classes.

       Texas has the potential to become a leader in data center development that will bring

significant economic benefits to the state. Rowan requests that the Commission harmonize the

PFP in this project with the Large Load Interconnection Rule to create a stable and competitive

environment for large-scale digital infrastructure in Texas that simultaneously meets the state’s

policy objectives to protect ratepayers from the cost impacts associated with growth in large load

interconnections. Rowan’s comments on the PFP focus on the following issues:

       (1) Minimum Billing Demand – Rowan supports a minimum billing demand charge and

           a regulatory scheme that provides for the reservation of capacity for large loads, but the

           charge should be calibrated to the transmission costs the load causes rather than set at

           a level that results in overcollection. Consistent with cost-causation principles and the

           policy goal of mitigating transmission rates for other customer classes, the duration and

           percentage used for the “large load minimum billing demand” in the PFP should be

           reduced from at least 20 years at full contracted peak demand to nine to 13 years at

           75% to 80% of contracted peak demand.

       (2) Transmission Interconnection Costs – The proposed definition of “transmission

           interconnection costs” in 16 TAC § 25.192(b)(13) and the exclusion of transmission

           interconnection costs from a TSP’s cost of service and rates in 16 TAC § 25.192(e)(6)

           would require that network upgrades be paid for directly by a large load, even if the

           upgrades can or would benefit the system. Direct assignment to large loads of network

           upgrade costs that provide system benefits would be a significant departure from the




                                                 4
          established Texas ratemaking practice and would create economic barriers for new

         large load customers, including data centers and manufacturing facilities, in the state.

         Such a change is not necessary to protect other customer classes if Commission rules

         require CIAC for direct costs that only benefit the large load customer (e.g., taps, bays,

         and breakers that serve the new load); financial security to cover system upgrades until

         customers energize; and a mandatory minimum billing demand at an amount and

         duration that covers the cost of capacity reserved for the customer.

      (3) TSP Tariff Requirements – Given the pre-energization requirements for CIAC and

         financial security in the Large Load Interconnection Rule and the minimum billing

         demand charge in this PFP, the proposed TSP tariff requirements in 16 TAC §

         25.252(d) should be revised so that the terms governing reallocation of transmission

         capacity are commensurate with the protections those requirements already provide.

      (4) Harmonization of the PFP and the Large Load Interconnection Rule - The PFP

         and the Large Load Interconnection Rule should be harmonized to avoid pancaking of

         charges and interconnection fees, and the direct assignment of system upgrade costs to

         large loads.


II.   RESPONSES TO THE COMMISSION’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS ON THE
                                   FOLLOWING QUESTIONS

1.    Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions

      be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or

      different non-coincident (NCP) demands?




                                               5
         RESPONSE:

        The Commission has the authority to differentiate minimum billing demand charges based

on load size. Commission rules require that customer classes be derived from electric service

characteristics.5 To the extent the Commission differentiates among large load customers, that

differentiation should turn on measurable electric service characteristics that bear on transmission

system impact, such as contracted peak demand in MW, load factor, and whether the customer is

dispatchable or registered as a controllable load resource, rather than on the identity or industry of

the customer.

        Importantly, any minimum billing demand tied to contracted peak demand for transmission

service should reflect only the capacity that the customer has contracted with the interconnecting

utility to serve and that is available to serve the load. Accordingly, Rowan requests that the

Commission confirm that the operational limits applicable to loads registered as provisional

controllable load resources (PCLRs) are properly reflected in the billing determinants ascribed to

those loads. Likewise, backup generating facilities and on-site generation disclosed under 16 TAC

§§ 25.194(d)(6) and (d)(7) should reduce, and not increase, a large load customer’s transmission

billing determinants.

2.      Should the large load minimum billing demand be:

                 A. fixed for 20 years as proposed;

                 B. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or

                 C. extended to a longer time period?




5
   See 16 TAC § 25.5(23) (defining a “Customer Class” as “[a] group of customers with similar electric-service
characteristics (e.g., residential, commercial, industrial, sales for resale) taking service under one or more rate
schedules.”).


                                                        6
        RESPONSE:

       None of the three options as proposed. To prevent cost shifting between customer classes,

Rowan supports a minimum billing demand construct because any large load that reserves

transmission capacity should pay for the capacity reserved for its load. Pre-energization, the load

should also post security to cover any network upgrades. However, a minimum billing demand

that takes effect as service becomes available should be calibrated to the transmission costs caused

by the load and should not result in overcollection from the customer or create a cost shift to or

from other customer classes.

       A permanent or very long demand ratchet, such as the proposed minimum of 20 years in

the PFP, raises policy and statutory concerns. A minimum billing demand obligation of that

duration is difficult to reconcile with cost-causation principles because it would likely result in

overcollection by the utility. It may also work against the reliability of the ERCOT grid by

dampening the large load customer’s incentives to pursue energy efficiency, provide demand

response, or invest in on-site generation, contravening Texas’ policy goals to promote on-site

generation from large load customers.

       Rowan recommends that the Commission adjust the proposed 20-year minimum billing

demand obligation to a duration and level that more closely align with cost causation. Rowan has

also reviewed the study provided by the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) in response to the

PFP and generally supports a nine- to 13-year minimum billing demand obligation set at 75% to

80% of contracted peak demand, with the duration depending on the percentage the Commission

selects. A minimum billing demand based on the results of the TEBA study would align costs

associated with large load capacity reservations with appropriate demand charges in line with

Texas’ long standing cost causation policy goals.




                                                 7
           To algin costs with capacity requests, Rowan also recommends that the Commission

require the offsets in 16 TAC §§ 25.192(k)(1) and (k)(2) to be reflected in the calculation of a large

load customer’s minimum billing demand obligation, so that a large load customer whose

interconnection fee and forfeited security have already reduced the TSP’s revenue requirement is

not charged a second time for the same facilities under the minimum billing demand requirements.

Such a result would be inconsistent with long-standing cost-causation principles and would

produce an unreasonable pancaking of rates.

          Further, whatever demand ratchet period the Commission adopts should be applied on a

per-phase basis for projects energizing in phases under an approved schedule for phased

energization, referred to in these comments as a load commissioning plan (LCP), so that the

obligation for each increment of capacity runs from the date that increment is constructed, tested,

and made available for service. This phased approach mirrors the Commission’s long-standing

requirement that assets be used and useful before cost recovery begins. 6

3.        Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand

          lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the

          large load minimum billing demand:

                 A. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing

                     demand is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or

                     maximum NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet

                     percentage decline in phases over the years, and how?

                 B. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the

                     large load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large



6
    See PURA § 36.051.


                                                  8
                    load customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the

                   previous year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should

                   the percentage weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP

                   demand decline in phases over the years, and how?

       RESPONSE:

       Yes, as described in response to Question 3. As stated above, the minimum billing demand

should be based on 75% to 80% of contracted peak demand, with the percentage varying based on

the duration of the obligation.

4.     Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as

       an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection

       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power

       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and

       cryptocurrency mining facilities?       Responses to this question should include

       applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large

       computational loads.

       RESPONSE:

       No.    Separate rate treatment should not be applied based on whether a load is

computational. A class defined by whether 50% or more of the demand at a site consists of power

electronic-based load is contrary to PURA’s mandate to provide non-discriminatory transmission

service. Such a class would also set a precedent for industry-specific rate design in ERCOT that

is untethered from cost causation. Commission rules expressly define a “customer class” as “[a]

group of customers with similar electric-service characteristics (e.g., residential, commercial,




                                               9
 industrial, sales for resale) taking service under one or more rate schedules.” 7           Once the

Commission classifies customers by the nature of their business rather than by their service

characteristics, there is no limiting principle for future classifications. PURA § 36.003 requires

electric rates to be just and reasonable and not unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or

discriminatory, and to be sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each customer class.

Although the Commission classifies end users based on the size or variability of their load, those

classifications are neutrally applied and grounded in the principle that customers of different sizes

have different electric service requirements. Creating a system in which loads with the same size

and variability characteristics are treated differently under the Commission’s rules would untether

electric regulation under PURA from cost-causation principles and would raise the discrimination

concerns PURA is designed to prevent.

          Furthermore, enforcing such a distinction would be administratively expensive and unduly

burdensome. It would require the DSP or ERCOT to characterize equipment behind the meter, to

monitor changes in that mix over time, and to resolve disputes about the composition of load at a

site, none of which bears on the cost the customer imposes on the transmission system. A

computational load class would also be in tension with SB 6, which directs the Commission to

establish large load interconnection standards in a manner designed to support business

development in this state. Singling out the specific industries would work against that directive.

          Finally, the proposed classification is inconsistent with the Commission’s own approach

in Project No. 58481, where 16 TAC §§ 25.194(b) and 25.194(c)(9) define the applicability of the

Large Load Interconnection Rule solely by reference to 75 MW of non-coincident peak demand

at a single site, without regard to the customer’s industry or the composition of its load. If the



7
    16 TAC § 25.5(23).


                                                 10
 Commission nonetheless determines that some form of differentiated treatment is warranted, the

line should be drawn by size rather than by end use. In short, PURA is best read to require that

differentiated ratemaking treatment be tied to neutral load characteristics such as size and

variability rather than to the nature of the equipment operating behind the point of delivery.

5.      Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include

        transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to

        serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

        RESPONSE:

        No. The definition of “transmission interconnection costs” should not be broadened to

sweep in transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study. Doing so would

convert network facilities that benefit the entire ERCOT system into a customer-funded obligation,

departing from the cost-allocation principle that has supported ERCOT’s growth. Instead, the

definition should be narrowed and clarified so that it captures only those facilities that can be used

solely by the interconnecting large load customer and expressly excludes system upgrades,

consistent with existing precedent governing transmission cost of service.

             A. The existing allocation of interconnection costs and system upgrade costs is

                 sound and should be preserved when coupled with CIAC, financial security,

                 and minimum billing demand requirements.

        Under the framework the Commission has proposed across Project Nos. 58000 and 58481,

a large load customer already bears substantial, layered financial responsibility for its

interconnection. It pays CIAC for direct interconnection costs — i.e. the facilities that serve only

that specific large load customer — under 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9). 8 It separately posts financial


8
 See Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9) (requiring a large load customer to pay all direct interconnection costs through
CIAC, with no standard or other allowance, not later than the date the interconnection agreement is executed).


                                                        11
 security for system upgrades necessary to reliably serve it under 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(10), which

is refunded in part upon energization and ratably as the customer meets its phased energization

milestones, with the remaining balance refunded once the customer sustains operations for five

years at its contracted peak demand.9 Although duplicative of the purpose of that financial

security, the Large Load Interconnection Rule would also require the customer to pay a non-

refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand, which is applied

as an offset to the interconnecting TSP’s rate base.10 And under the proposed rules in this project,

the large load customer must satisfy a large load minimum billing demand for a period no less than

20 years — including 240 consecutive payments during the first 20 years after commencement of

billing, based on the greater of its contracted peak demand, its highest non-coincident peak demand

in the past year, or its 12CP demand — to reserve transmission capacity, whether or not it has

energized or is fully using that capacity.11

        Taken together, that package of pancaked charges would recover substantially more

revenue from the large load customer than the costs the customer causes to the system as a direct

result of its interconnection. It would assign to the customer the full cost of the facilities dedicated

to it, secure the risk of nonperformance on system upgrades through financial security, add a non-

refundable per-MW interconnection fee, and then require a revenue commitment of at least two

decades on top of those obligations. Security for system upgrades, rather than CIAC for system

upgrades, is the correct instrument: it protects other customers against stranded investment without

permanently assigning the cost of a network asset to a single customer. Rowan respectfully




9
   Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(i)(1)-(2).
10
    Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7).
11
    Proposed 16 TAC § 25.252(e)(2); see also proposed 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(2)-(3).



                                                      12
 submits that there is no gap in cost recovery that a broadened definition of transmission

interconnection costs is needed to fill.


     B. Network facilities benefit the entire ERCOT system, and cost responsibility should

          follow who can use a facility, not who happens to connect first.

          The distinction that matters is not whether a facility appears on a batch study output, but

whether the facility can ever be used to serve anyone other than the requesting customer. Facilities

that will only ever serve a single load — the tap, bay, and breaker that directly serve the new load

— are properly recovered through CIAC. Facilities that are or could be used by other customers

in the future are network facilities that provide system benefits, and their costs should be shared

by all users through transmission rates.

          Oncor’s comments in Project No. 58481 illustrate the point.12 A ten-mile radial line built

to serve a new load is not owned by that load; it is a piece of the ERCOT grid available for public

service, and the utility will serve any later customer that wishes to tap it. Charging the first

customer CIAC for the entirety of that system-wide investment would be inequitable and would

price the first mover out of the market, stifling economic development throughout the ERCOT

region.

     C. Broadening the definition would create a first-mover problem and invite the

          interconnection delays experienced in other markets.

          Assigning batch-study-driven network costs solely to the customers in that batch places the

cost of grid-wide benefits on the shoulders of a single incremental customer or a small group of

them. Such a system would result in a first-mover penalty, contrary to the purpose of PURA §


12
   Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA § 37.0561, Project No. 58481,
Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC’s Comments on the Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC § 25.194 at 3
(Apr. 17, 2026).


                                                   13
 37.0561, which directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards in a manner

designed to support business development in Texas. 13 Regional transmission organizations that

have imposed network upgrade cost responsibility on interconnecting customers in the generation

context — SPP and MISO — have been plagued by project cancellations and multi-year

interconnection delays.14

          The batch study process makes the problem worse, not better. When multiple large loads

are modeled together in a single batch, there is no reasonable way to discern which customer

caused a given system upgrade. Further, it is unknown whether another user of the transmission

system (e.g., generators, other TSPs and DSPs, or other large loads) will benefit. The extent to

which a particular customer “uses” a transmission asset cannot be conclusively modeled: grid

modeling evaluates many contingencies and scenarios, and one scenario may show a load using

nearly all of an upgrade’s capacity while another shows it using little to none. Determinations of

that kind are inherently contestable and would generate contested cases or restudies by ERCOT

that would delay the interconnection of every load behind them. Once costs are assigned to an

individual customer, it is not uncommon for that customer to drop out of the study based on the

increased costs, potentially triggering cascading restudies and further delaying development.

          Reallocation as later customers or wholesale users of the system (e.g., generators) arrive

compounds the difficulty. If subsequent interconnecting customers were required to fund already-

funded upgrades, the utility would have to refund a portion of the original customers’ contributions

and shift responsibility forward — tracking net book value, contracted peak demand shares, and



13
     PURA § 37.0561(b).
14
  See, e.g., Why Interconnection Queues Remain the Biggest Roadblock to Renewable Projects, ZERO-EMISSION
GRID (Oct. 3, 2025) (“Even when studies are completed, projects often face prohibitive network upgrade costs.
Developers in regions like PJM, MISO, and SPP are finding upgrades in the hundreds of millions of dollars, making
many projects financially unviable.”), https://www.zeroemissiongrid.com/zeg-blog/queue-backlog/.


                                                       14
 asset-by-asset credits, often for loads that have changed hands two or three times in the interim.

Utilities should devote their resources to providing service, not to administering a clearinghouse

of customer credits. ERCOT’s transmission rate design has served Texas well precisely because

it avoids protracted, facility-by-facility disputes over cost responsibility for assets whose users

cannot be predicted over a multi-decade service life.

   D. If the Commission nevertheless broadens the definition, it should do so narrowly and

       pair it with a reimbursement mechanism.

       Rowan does not support broadening the definition. If the Commission proceeds, however,

two guardrails are essential.

       First, any expansion should be limited to transmission facilities that are functionally radial

to an identified customer and that provide no current or reasonably foreseeable future benefit to

the broader ERCOT transmission system. Facilities that relieve pre-existing constraints, provide

broader system benefits, or would have been constructed to serve current or future regional load

growth should remain in the TSP’s transmission cost of service and be recovered through rates.

The Commission should make that distinction explicit in the rule text rather than leaving it to case-

by-case determination.

       Second, where facilities initially assigned to a batch are later used to serve additional

customers (whether large load or other users of the transmission system), the Commission should

require a pro rata refund or credit to the original funding customers, calculated on remaining net

book value. Absent such a mechanism, the first mover in a load pocket permanently subsidizes

every subsequent entrant, and cost responsibility is divorced from actual use.




                                                 15
       E. The Commission should confirm that system upgrades remain in transmission cost of

          service and should harmonize its interconnection cost terminology across the

          proposals in Project No. 58000 and Project No. 58481.

          Two clarifications would materially reduce future disputes.

          First, the Commission should confirm that system upgrades remain recoverable through

the TSP’s transmission cost of service and are not converted into a customer-funded obligation by

operation of proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(e)(6) — which excludes transmission interconnection

costs associated with interconnection agreements signed after the rule’s effective date from a

TSP’s transmission cost of service — read together with proposed 16 TAC § 25.252(c)(2), which

requires a large load customer to pay CIAC for transmission interconnection costs and distribution

interconnection costs.15 The interaction of those provisions, combined with a broadened definition

of transmission interconnection costs, is the mechanism by which network costs could be shifted

onto large load customers without the Commission ever squarely deciding to do so.

          Second, the Commission should adopt a single set of defined terms for interconnection

costs and use them consistently across 16 TAC §§ 25.192, 25.193, 25.194, and 25.252. The

proposed rules currently use “transmission interconnection costs” and “distribution

interconnection costs,” each defined in proposed § 25.252(b), alongside “direct interconnection

costs” in proposed § 25.194(f)(9), which is not separately defined. 16 Rowan recommends that the

Commission define “direct interconnection costs” to mean the costs of facilities that can be used

only to serve the interconnecting large load customer — including the tap, bay, and breaker directly

serving that customer — and use that term consistently in place of the current mix of terminology.


15
     Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(e)(6); proposed 16 TAC § 25.252(c)(2).
16
     Proposed 16 TAC § 25.252(b)(2), (b)(5); proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9).

 6.        If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of

          whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,

          how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments

          and transmission planning studies?

          RESPONSE:

          Reserved capacity should be reflected, and it should be reflected using the LCP that the

Large Load Interconnection Rule and Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145, already

require the large load customer to provide.17 That schedule is the most reliable available indication

of when reserved capacity will convert to actual load. For transmission planning studies, ERCOT

should reflect the full contracted peak demand under an executed interconnection agreement. That

is the quantity the customer has committed to, has posted financial security against, and is being

billed on. Planning to a lower number would defeat the purpose of the reservation and risk under-

building the network. For resource adequacy reports and assessments and for operational demand

forecasting, ERCOT should instead use the load characteristics included in each large load’s LCP.

This approach recognizes the reserved transmission commitment for planning purposes while

ensuring that near-term reliability assessments and load forecasts reflect the expected timing of

actual load, rather than assuming instantaneous energization of the full contracted peak demand.

Resource adequacy assessments should also reflect the backup generating facilities, on-site

generation, and controllable load resource capability disclosed under 16 TAC §§ 25.194(d)(6)

through (d)(8), which materially affect the net contribution of a large load to system peak.

          Relatedly, the Commission should define the term “available service.”                Rowan

recommends that 16 TAC §§ 25.192(f)(1)(B), 25.193(d)(3), and 25.252(e)(1) each state that, for a



17
     Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.194(d)(5) & (f)(5); ERCOT Planning Guide §§ 9.2.1.1 & 9.2.1.2.


                                                       17
 project with an LCP under 16 TAC § 25.194, available service means only the transmission

capacity that has been constructed, tested, and made available for service under the applicable

phase of the LCP. This clarification harmonizes the implementation of Project No. 58000 and

Project No. 58481 and ensures that transmission planning, resource adequacy, and billing all

reflect the same staged delivery of capacity.


          III.       ADDITIONAL COMMENTS AND REDLINES TO THE PFP

   Rowan offers the following additional comments and proposed redlines to the PFP consistent
with the responses above:

           A. Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(b): Definition of “Direct Interconnection Costs”

                 (2)(13)      Transmission         interconnection         costsDirect

                 Interconnection Costs -- All costs associated with the facilities

                 required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection

                 of a transmission-level customer, or a distinct set of transmission-

                 level customers, to the existing transmission network, including

                 interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and

                 associated equipment necessary to establish or modify service.The

                 costs associated with facilities that are used exclusively to serve the

                 interconnecting large load customer, including but not limited to, the

                 tap, bay, and breaker equipment directly serving that customer. The

                 term does not include facilities that could be used to serve any other

                 customer or user of the transmission system, including but not

                 limited to facilities that relieve pre-existing constraints, provide




                                                   18
    broader system benefits, or would have been constructed to serve

   current or future load growth.


B. Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(e)(6): Exclusion of Direct Interconnection Costs

   from TCOS

   (6) Notwithstanding any other provision of this section,

   transmission interconnection costsDirect Interconnection Costs

   associated with interconnection agreements signed after the

   effective date of this section must not be included in a TSP’s

   transmission cost of service or transmission service rates.


C. Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(f)(1)(B): Available Service for Billing Units

   (B) Notwithstanding the applicability of §25.193 of this title

   (relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost

   Recovery Factor (TCRF)), ERCOT must perform adjustments to

   each DSP 12CP load value by adding to each measured DSP 12CP

   load, for each large load customer of that DSP, the difference

   between that customer’s large load minimum billing demand, as

   described in §25.193 of this title (relating to Distribution Service

   Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF)), and that

           K. Harmonization With Large Load Interconnection Rule

                    1. Inconsistent cost terminology.

       This proposal uses "transmission interconnection costs" in 16 TAC §§ 25.192(b)(13) and

25.252(b)(5) and "distribution interconnection costs" in 16 TAC § 25.252(b)(2), while 16 TAC §

25.194(f)(9)(A) uses "direct interconnection costs" to describe the facilities built to interconnect

the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system. Three overlapping terms across two rules

 governing the same payments will produce disputes over what a customer must fund through

CIAC. Rowan recommends the Commission adopt defined terms that are used consistently in all

new large load interconnection rules. Specifically, the term "direct interconnection costs," as

defined in 16 TAC §§ 25.192(b)(13) and 25.252(b) of this title, must be used as the single defined

term for the costs of facilities that can be used only to serve the interconnecting large load customer

across 16 TAC §§ 25.192, 25.193, 25.194, and 25.252.

                   2. Treatment of network system upgrades.

        The large load interconnection rule distinguishes direct interconnection costs, which are

paid through CIAC under 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9), from system upgrades, which are secured by

financial security under 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(10) but are not made a CIAC obligation. Proposed

16 TAC § 25.252(c)(2) requires CIAC for all transmission interconnection costs and distribution

interconnection costs, and 16 TAC § 25.192(e)(6) excludes transmission interconnection costs

from a TSP' s transmission cost of service for agreements signed after the effective date. Read

together, it is unclear whether network system upgrades remain rate based. Rowan recommends

the Commission confirm that system upgrades that provide network benefits remain in the TSP' s

transmission cost of service and are not converted into a CIAC obligation.
